title: Pulmonary Function Testing: Obstruction, Restriction, and the Question the Test Can Answer
bottomLine: Interpret pulmonary function tests by pattern and clinical question. Spirometry identifies airflow obstruction and bronchodilator response; low FVC alone does not prove restriction, and diffusion capacity adds a separate gas-transfer clue. Never diagnose asthma, COPD or interstitial disease from one number without symptoms, exposure history and test quality.
recognize: A reduced expiratory ratio supports airflow obstruction when measured with valid technique and appropriate reference equations.
A low FVC can reflect true restriction, air trapping or poor effort; lung volumes are needed to confirm restriction.
Reduced DLCO can occur with emphysema, pulmonary vascular disease or interstitial disease, while asthma often preserves diffusion capacity.
differentiate: Bronchodilator responsiveness supports variable airflow physiology but a negative response does not exclude asthma.
Race/ethnicity should not be used as a simplistic biologic correction for pulmonary function interpretation; use current reference standards and clinical context.
assessment: Confirm indication, symptoms, smoking/vaping and occupational exposure, inhaler timing, recent infection/exacerbation and ability to perform acceptable manoeuvres.
workup: Review acceptability/reproducibility before interpreting values, then integrate spirometry, lung volumes and DLCO according to the diagnostic question.
Use bronchoprovocation, imaging or specialty testing only when the clinical question remains unresolved.
management: Use the pattern to refine diagnosis and treatment, not to replace the history and examination.
Refer unexplained restriction, disproportionate DLCO reduction, rapidly changing lung function or diagnostically discordant findings to respiratory care.
medicationSafety: Document bronchodilator withholding or recent use when it affects interpretation.
Do not escalate inhaled therapy solely because a single technically poor spirometry value looks worse.
redFlags: Disproportionately low DLCO with pulmonary vascular concern
New severe obstruction with respiratory distress
counselling: Explain that PFTs describe physiology; the diagnosis comes from physiology plus the clinical story.
followUp: Repeat testing when a defined management question exists, such as response, progression or diagnostic clarification.
examTrap: Calling a low FVC 'restrictive lung disease' without confirming restriction with lung volumes.
oneLinePearl: Spirometry shows airflow; lung volumes prove restriction; DLCO adds gas-transfer information.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Function Testing guidance

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Prescribe a Target, Reassess the Need
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug for hypoxemia, not a routine treatment for dyspnea with normal oxygenation. In acute illness, titrate to an appropriate target and reassess; long-term/home oxygen requires documented eligibility, stable-state assessment and equipment/safety planning rather than continuation by inertia.
recognize: Hypoxemia, not breathlessness alone, is the indication for supplemental oxygen.
Some patients with chronic hypercapnic respiratory disease require controlled oxygen targets and close reassessment rather than unrestricted high-flow oxygen.
differentiate: Oxygen does not treat the underlying cause of asthma, COPD exacerbation, PE, pneumonia or heart failure.
Short-term oxygen during an acute illness is not automatically an indication for permanent home oxygen.
assessment: Assess saturation, work of breathing, perfusion, mental status, baseline oxygen use, COPD/hypercapnia risk, smoking/fire risk and the cause of hypoxemia.
workup: Use arterial/venous gas testing when hypercapnia/acid-base status will change care and confirm stable-state home-oxygen eligibility according to the applicable Canadian program/guideline.
management: Titrate oxygen to the clinical target while treating the cause of hypoxemia and escalating respiratory support when oxygen alone is insufficient.
For home therapy, specify flow/device/conditions of use and arrange reassessment after clinically meaningful change.
medicationSafety: Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients; reassess gas exchange when clinically indicated rather than withholding necessary oxygen from a hypoxemic patient.
Oxygen supports combustion: active smoking/open-flame safety must be addressed explicitly.
counselling: Teach device use, fire safety, prescribed flow/target and that changing oxygen cannot substitute for urgent assessment when breathing worsens.
followUp: Reassess continuing oxygen need, adherence/device function and the underlying cardiopulmonary disease.
examTrap: Giving oxygen simply because a patient feels short of breath despite normal saturation—or continuing home oxygen indefinitely after transient acute hypoxemia without reassessment.
oneLinePearl: Prescribe oxygen for hypoxemia with a target and a reassessment plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society home oxygen and respiratory guidance

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Low-Dose CT for the Right Asymptomatic Risk Group
bottomLine: Lung-cancer screening is for asymptomatic people at elevated smoking-related risk and uses low-dose CT through current provincial/territorial eligibility pathways. A patient with hemoptysis, persistent focal symptoms or other cancer alarm features needs diagnostic evaluation, not a screening referral.
recognize: Current Canadian public guidance supports low-dose CT screening for selected people with substantial current or former smoking exposure.
Eligibility and program implementation vary across provinces/territories and may use age, smoking duration/pack-years or validated risk models.
differentiate: Screening and diagnostic CT are different pathways; symptoms convert the encounter from screening to diagnosis.
Chest radiography and sputum cytology are not recommended substitutes for evidence-based low-dose CT screening.
assessment: Confirm absence of concerning symptoms, smoking history, age/risk-program eligibility, ability/willingness to undergo diagnostic follow-up and treatment, major competing illness and access barriers.
workup: Use the current provincial/territorial lung-screening pathway and its nodule/follow-up algorithm rather than importing a fixed interval from another jurisdiction.
management: Refer eligible asymptomatic patients into organized screening where available and integrate smoking-cessation support without making cessation a prerequisite for respectful care.
Abnormal LDCT results require closed-loop nodule/diagnostic follow-up.
medicationSafety: No medication replaces screening; avoid sedating premedication or unnecessary invasive testing before imaging findings warrant it.
counselling: Discuss benefits, false positives, incidental findings, radiation and overdiagnosis, and explain why screening applies before symptoms appear.
followUp: Track every abnormal screen to definitive resolution and update the next screening interval from the program recommendation.
examTrap: Ordering a screening LDCT for a patient with hemoptysis instead of beginning a diagnostic lung-cancer workup.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms: screen eligible risk; symptoms: diagnose.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cancer Society lung cancer screening guidance
Provincial and territorial lung screening programs

title: Allergic Rhinitis and Rhinosinusitis: Treat the Pattern, Avoid Reflex Antibiotics
bottomLine: Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory upper-airway syndrome managed with trigger control and effective intranasal therapy. Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral; reserve antibiotics for a compatible bacterial pattern or complication rather than treating coloured mucus or facial pressure alone.
recognize: Allergic rhinitis commonly causes sneezing, itch, watery rhinorrhea and congestion with ocular symptoms/seasonal or exposure pattern.
Bacterial rhinosinusitis is more plausible with persistent nonimproving symptoms, severe onset or clear double-worsening rather than the first few days of a URI.
differentiate: Migraine, dental disease, structural obstruction and medication-related rhinitis can mimic 'sinus headache'.
Chronic rhinosinusitis requires persistent symptoms plus objective evidence through ENT pathways, not repeated acute antibiotic courses.
assessment: Assess duration/pattern, allergy triggers, asthma, unilateral symptoms, epistaxis, dental pain, fever, orbital/neurologic symptoms and medication/decongestant use.
workup: Routine imaging is unnecessary for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis; use allergy testing or ENT imaging/endoscopy when the result will change chronic/refractory management.
management: Use intranasal corticosteroid and/or antihistamine strategies matched to allergic symptoms plus saline where helpful.
Provide supportive care for uncomplicated viral sinusitis and guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy only when bacterial disease is reasonably likely.
medicationSafety: Topical decongestant overuse can cause rebound congestion; systemic decongestants may worsen hypertension/palpitations and have pregnancy considerations.
Avoid repeated antibiotics for chronic nasal symptoms without confirming the diagnosis.
redFlags: Severe frontal headache or neurologic signs
counselling: Teach correct intranasal spray technique and explain why coloured mucus alone does not prove bacterial infection.
followUp: Reassess persistent/recurrent disease for asthma/allergy control, adherence/technique, structural disease or ENT referral.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for three days of congestion and green nasal discharge without a bacterial time course or complication.
oneLinePearl: Upper-airway colour is not culture; pattern and duration decide whether sinusitis is bacterial.

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Decide Who Needs Imaging and Antibiotics
bottomLine: Most uncomplicated acute bronchitis is viral and does not benefit from antibiotics. The NP decision is whether vitals, oxygenation, focal lung findings, age/comorbidity and illness severity make pneumonia plausible enough to require imaging or antimicrobial treatment.
recognize: Acute cough after a viral prodrome with normal oxygenation/vitals and no focal consolidation usually fits bronchitis/viral URI.
Pneumonia becomes more plausible with fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal crackles/bronchial breath sounds, pleuritic pain or systemic illness.
differentiate: Purulent sputum can occur in viral bronchitis and does not independently prove bacterial infection.
Older/frail or immunocompromised adults may have pneumonia without high fever and require a lower threshold for evaluation.
assessment: Assess respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, HR/BP, focal chest findings, hydration, mental status, age/frailty and cardiopulmonary/immune comorbidity.
workup: Avoid routine chest X-ray in a low-risk patient with normal vital signs and lung examination; obtain imaging when pneumonia remains clinically plausible or the patient is higher risk.
management: Provide symptom care and return precautions for uncomplicated bronchitis; do not use routine antibiotics.
When pneumonia is confirmed/strongly suspected, use current Canadian/local CAP treatment and disposition guidance matched to severity/comorbidity.
medicationSafety: Unnecessary antibiotics cause adverse effects, C. difficile and resistance without shortening routine bronchitis meaningfully.
Avoid routine opioid antitussive/sedative combinations in older or respiratory-vulnerable patients.
redFlags: Failure to improve/worsening after expected viral course
counselling: Set expectations for cough duration and give explicit return precautions; explain why antibiotics do not treat most bronchitis.
followUp: Reassess if dyspnea, persistent fever, hemoptysis or worsening symptoms develop.
examTrap: Using sputum colour as the deciding reason to prescribe an antibiotic for acute bronchitis.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis is usually a cough syndrome; pneumonia is a lung-parenchymal illness supported by severity and focal findings.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Antibiotics Wisely

title: Occupational Lung Disease: Make the Exposure Timeline Part of the Diagnosis
bottomLine: Occupational respiratory disease is often missed because exposure history is too generic. Identify the agent, intensity/duration, latency and work-versus-away symptom pattern, stabilize urgent disease, and connect diagnosis to exposure reduction, occupational medicine and appropriate reporting/compensation systems without making legal causation claims from one visit.
recognize: Work-related asthma may improve away from work and worsen during shifts; sensitizers can cause disease even at low later exposures after sensitization.
Silica/asbestos/metal/organic dust exposures can cause chronic interstitial, pleural, airway or malignant disease with long latency.
differentiate: Smoking-related COPD, idiopathic ILD, infection and environmental/home exposures can coexist and must not automatically displace an occupational cause.
A normal chest X-ray does not exclude occupational asthma or early exposure-related disease.
assessment: Ask exact job tasks, substances, ventilation/PPE, duration, symptom timing during/after work, coworkers with symptoms, prior jobs and nonoccupational exposures.
Assess acute inhalation injury, oxygenation and irritant exposure that may require emergency care.
workup: Use serial peak-flow/spirometry patterns, bronchoprovocation, imaging and exposure-specific testing through occupational/respirology pathways as clinically appropriate.
Document exposure history precisely because later occupational-health decisions depend on it.
management: Remove/reduce hazardous exposure when disease is suspected and coordinate workplace/occupational medicine assessment while treating the respiratory condition.
Use applicable provincial occupational-health/reporting systems and avoid sending the patient back into a known dangerous exposure without a safety plan.
medicationSafety: Medication can control symptoms but does not make a harmful exposure safe; escalating inhalers without addressing the workplace can permit progression.
Use respiratory protective equipment as part of a hierarchy of controls, not as the sole solution when elimination/substitution/engineering controls are possible.
counselling: Encourage patients to record exposures and work/symptom timing and explain that occupational evaluation may require workplace information and longitudinal testing.
followUp: Ensure respiratory and occupational-health referral, exposure modification and pending diagnostic results are closed-loop.
examTrap: Treating recurrent workplace-triggered wheeze as ordinary asthma while never asking what the patient inhales at work.
oneLinePearl: For occupational lung disease, the exposure timeline is part of the physical exam.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society occupational respiratory guidance

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Diagnose the Risk, Then Make PAP Usable
bottomLine: OSA is recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep causing physiologic stress and fragmented sleep. Screening tools estimate probability but do not diagnose OSA; confirm with an appropriate sleep study, then treat severity, symptoms and comorbidity while troubleshooting PAP adherence rather than declaring therapy failure after one poor mask experience.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia and daytime sleepiness are common but absence of sleepiness does not exclude clinically important OSA.
OSA increases driving/work risk when excessive sleepiness is present.
differentiate: Insomnia, restless legs, narcolepsy, circadian disorders, medication sedation and insufficient sleep can produce daytime fatigue/sleepiness.
Central sleep apnea is physiologically different and requires another diagnostic pathway.
assessment: Assess snoring/apneas, sleepiness, driving risk, BMI/neck/anatomy, resistant hypertension/AF/HF, sedating medications/alcohol, sleep schedule and occupation.
workup: Use validated screening to identify risk, then home sleep apnea testing or polysomnography according to pretest probability, comorbidity and the local sleep pathway.
Do not use overnight oximetry alone as a universal definitive OSA test.
management: Use PAP for appropriate moderate/severe or symptomatic/high-risk disease and troubleshoot mask fit, humidification, pressure comfort and nasal obstruction.
Address weight, alcohol/sedative exposure, positional factors and oral appliance/surgical options when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Sedatives/opioids can worsen sleep-disordered breathing and driving risk; review them explicitly.
Do not prescribe wake-promoting medication for persistent sleepiness before confirming adequate sleep and effective OSA treatment.
redFlags: Significant cardiopulmonary comorbidity with complex sleep-disordered breathing
Persistent hypoxemia not explained by OSA alone
counselling: Discuss driving safety and explain that PAP benefit depends on effective nightly use, not simply owning the device.
followUp: Review objective PAP use/efficacy, symptoms, mask/interface issues and cardiovascular/metabolic comorbidity.
examTrap: Calling a high STOP-Bang score a diagnosis or abandoning PAP without first troubleshooting why the patient cannot use it.
oneLinePearl: Screening finds OSA risk; sleep testing diagnoses it; adherence work makes PAP effective.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society guidance

title: Pulmonary Nodule: Risk-Stratify the Finding, Do Not Call It Cancer or Ignore It
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule needs structured malignancy-risk assessment using size, morphology, growth, smoking/exposure history and patient factors. Compare prior imaging, use the applicable nodule pathway, and own the follow-up; a screening-program nodule and a symptomatic diagnostic presentation are not interchangeable.
recognize: Larger size, spiculation, upper-lobe location, growth and smoking/cancer history increase malignancy probability.
Many small nodules are benign, but failure to close follow-up can delay a curable cancer.
differentiate: Solitary nodule management differs from diffuse infection/inflammatory nodules and from a lung mass with symptoms/adenopathy.
Do not apply an incidental-nodule surveillance table blindly to a known cancer patient, immunocompromised patient or organized screening-program result when another pathway applies.
assessment: Review prior imaging, smoking/exposure history, cancer history, immune status, systemic symptoms, hemoptysis and whether the finding arose through screening or diagnostic imaging.
workup: Compare all prior chest imaging and use current Canadian/local radiology or screening algorithms to determine interval CT, PET/CT, biopsy or specialty referral.
Avoid immediate invasive biopsy of every low-risk small nodule when evidence-based surveillance is appropriate.
management: Create a documented follow-up owner/date before the encounter closes and refer suspicious/growing/high-risk nodules to the appropriate lung diagnostic pathway.
Smoking cessation is beneficial but does not replace imaging follow-up.
medicationSafety: No medication treats an undiagnosed nodule; avoid empiric repeated antibiotics or corticosteroids solely to see whether a suspicious nodule disappears unless an infectious/inflammatory diagnosis is clinically supported.
counselling: Explain that most nodules are not cancer while emphasizing why interval imaging or diagnostic follow-up must not be missed.
followUp: Track imaging to completion and act on growth or changed risk; document resolution when surveillance ends.
examTrap: Telling a patient the nodule is cancer—or harmless—before risk stratification and prior-imaging comparison.
oneLinePearl: A pulmonary nodule is a risk-management problem until follow-up proves what it is.
sourceBasis: Canadian lung nodule and lung cancer diagnostic practice
